news.title: Germany’s far-right AfD set for big win in eastern state, just short of majority
news.text:
Germany's Alternative for Germany (AfD) is heading for a big victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, far ahead of its mainstream rivals, according to incomplete results. 

Projections indicate it is set to fall short of a majority, but the AfD says it has won a mandate to govern.

The far-right AfD is set to win a record 44% of the vote, well ahead of the conservative CDU on just over 17%.

The AfD's charismatic leader in the state, Ulrich Siegmund, said it was "sensational" and they wanted to start governing as soon as possible.

No far-right party has won control of a German state since World War Two, and governing at state level would mean powers over policing, local education and culture.

Saxony-Anhalt has a small population of 2.1 million and the AfD in the state is assessed by domestic intelligence as "right-wing extremist", a classification rejected by Siegmund, 35.

With more than 97% of the votes counted, the AfD is on track to score more than double its result in 2021, and Siegmund along with joint national leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla were overjoyed as the news emerged.

Commentators and political opponents spoke of the outcome as a watershed and break with the past. Main TV channel Das Erste cancelled its legendary crime drama Tatort to focus on what the result meant.

"This isn't just about Saxony-Anhalt," Siegmund told supporters. "It's a signal for the whole of Germany - a self-confident signal."

US President Donald Trump posted a screenshot of the German TV projection on his Truth Social platform, and then Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev took a screengrab of Trump's post and praised a "historic win for the pragmatic AfD".

Dmitriev had earlier praised the Russia-friendly AfD as "the party of hope and reason, co-operation truth and hope for Germany". Ahead of Germany's federal election last year, US Vice-President JD Vance endorsed the party, in a move criticised in Germany as political interference.

Without enough seats to form a majority government, Ulrich Siegmund has so far refused to lead a minority government, even though the party's national leaders see it as a possibility.

"If necessary there'll just be new elections, then we'd just get 50 or 55%," said Siegmund, while saying he was prepared to work with individual MPs or a party.

For hours it was unclear whether the BSW would reach the 5% threshold needed to enter parliament, although interim results showed it had succeeded. Had it failed, then the AfD would have seen its chances of a majority increase.

The AfD is currently heading for 39 seats in the 83-seat state parliament.

A crowd of supporters at the AfD election night party HQ erupted in cheers as the projections came up on the screen.

A short while later, people burst into singing Germany's national anthem.

"We have made history in this state," Siegmund said. His opposite number in the CDU, Sven Schulze, conceded victory and said his party would have to deal with the result: "This was an extremely tough and intensive election campaign."

Germany's centre-left SPD described the outcome as "truly dramatic" and national leader Lars Klingbeil, whose party is in government nationally with the CDU, described the outcome as a "signal to Berlin" and he was adamant that they would hear it.

AfD stands for Alternative für Deutschland and is openly pro-Russia and anti-migration. It has not only dominated the election campaign, it is emerging as the dominant force in the result and its supporters believe they are on the march.

Turnout in Saxony-Anhalt was particularly high at up to 78%, and AfD supporters in Magdeburg praised Siegmund's success in winning over voters.

One man called Ollie said: "This man gives us what no-one else can give."

"No matter what government, they all just promise things to get better. This is a party for the working people. It is the alternative for Germany," he told the BBC.

Another AfD voter called Bert said people in the east could sense things were not going well: "Things need to improve for us, for my family - I have three children. I'm in fear, I'm really in fear that safety erodes more and more."

Other parties refuse to go into coalition with the AfD, operating a Brandmauer or firewall aimed at keeping the far right out of government. In Saxony-Anhalt, the BSW has offered to co-operate with the AfD on some issues if it gets into the state parliament.

The AfD leads the opinion polls nationally, ahead of the ruling conservatives of Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the Social Democrats, but their heartland lies in the eastern states.

They also won the 2024 state election in neighbouring Thuringia, but failed to secure enough seats to win power.

Among the AfD's policies is a highly controversial plan for "remigration", which is widely understood to mean mass deportations of migrants, although the party says it refers to deporting criminals and those in the country illegally. It would not be able to achieve either if it ran the government of one of 16 states.

But it would have significant local powers. The party has been particularly critical of the Bauhaus school of design which the Nazis shut down in the city of Dessau in Saxony-Anhalt after they came to power in 1933. The AfD has called it "the dead-end of modernism", prompting some to accuse the party of using similar language to the Nazis.

Nikita, a demonstrator at an anti-AfD "Democracy Festival" in Magdeburg on the eve of the vote said Germans had to "learn from our history and not go back. We don't want the dark times any more".

Responding to the news from Saxony-Anhalt, the veteran head of the Jewish community in Munich and Bavaria, Charlotte Knobloch, said it frightened her. "On days like this I find it hard to recognise my homeland any more," the 93-year-old Holocaust survivor said, appealing for mainstream parties not to stand by and allow "this decline".

One of the AfD's top figures in Saxony-Anhalt, Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, has also been criticised for his approach to Russia. When asked why he had a Russian army mug in his office, he said it was just a souvenir, and "it's not our war".
news.summary: Germany's Alternative for Germany (AfD) is heading for a big victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, far ahead of its mainstream rivals, according to incomplete results.
news.author: Abubakar Ibrahim

news.title: Armed man lunged at Democratic Ohio governor candidate, campaign says
news.text: An armed assailant lunged at the Democratic candidate for Ohio governor, Amy Acton, on Sunday during a campaign stop at the Canfield Fair, injuring several people, campaign officials said.The suspect knocked volunteers to the ground and was arrested with "multiple weapons," Mahoning County Democratic Party Chairman Chris Anderson said in a statement.Acton was not injured, but campaign officials said multiple people were hurt.Acton was "grateful for the swift and decisive action of law enforcement and are praying for the recovery of those injured. This kind of violence has no place in Ohio. Dr. Acton will always stand up to the chaos, hate and vitriol that pits us against one another," said Addie Bullock, communications director for the campaign.Acton is facing Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, who has parlayed his national name recognition, tech industry connections and alliance with President Donald Trump into a record fundraising haul that he is tapping for advertising spots aimed at the November election. He is using campaign rallies and advertising to criticize Acton, the state's former public health director.Ramaswamy called the incident on Sunday unacceptable."Candidates should be able to meet with voters without having to worry about threats or violence. What happened today is completely unacceptable and has no place in politics, and we hope that no one was hurt," Ramaswamy's communications director, Connie Luck, said in a statement Sunday.The fairground's police department referred inquiries to the Mahoning County Sheriff's Department, which didn't immediately return a message seeking comment. The Ohio State Highway Patrol didn't immediately respond to a request for information.
news.summary: Several people were injured when an armed assailant lunged at Amy Acton, the Democratic candidate for Ohio governor, during a campaign stop at the Canfield Fair, campaign officials said.

news.title: Trump makes false claim about Bank of Canada while defending Canada tariffs
news.text:
US President Donald Trump appeared to mistake the Bank of Canada for a commercial bank while criticising Canada’s banking system and defending his tariffs on the country.

Speaking at an Oval Office event on Wednesday, Trump claimed Canada allows its banks to operate in the United States while blocking American banks from operating north of the border.

“They have their banks here, Bank of Canada, all of their big banks, big beautiful banks,” Trump said, according to CBC News.

“We don't have our banks there. You know why? They don't allow it.”

The Bank of Canada, however, is Canada’s central bank and a Crown corporation and does not offer everyday consumer banking services or operate retail branches in the United States.

Trump’s broader claim that American banks are not allowed to operate in Canada is also false, CBC reported.

Several US financial institutions have Canadian operations, including JPMorganChase and Citibank. Foreign-owned banks with Canadian subsidiaries operate under Canada’s Schedule 2 banking category.

Canada’s banking industry is dominated by six major domestic institutions: Royal Bank, Bank of Montreal, Scotiabank, CIBC, TD Bank and National Bank.

news.title: Police Group Blue Lives Matter Drops Jelly Roll from Mar-a-Lago Fundraiser Event
news.text:
National police organization Blue Lives Matter has disinvited Jelly Roll from its fundraising event at Mar-a-Lago after the country singer told supporters of President Donald Trump during a Jimmy Kimmel Live! monologue that he did not want them as fans and that they should stop listening to his music.

The singer, whose real name is Jason Bradley DeFord, unleashed his invective toward Republicans, MAGA fans, and President Trump and his supporters while filling in on ABC for Kimmel. Jelly Roll blasted Trump for his part in the Freedom 250 Grand Prix, called the president a “fat pig,” and insinuated Trump is a racist. In subsequent days Jelly Roll went even farther. And fans were not amused.

Now, the backlash is continuing as the planners of the pro-police fundraiser have removed Jelly Roll from their guest performer list.

The Police Tribune owner Kyle S. Reyes took to his X account on Friday to tell the singer “We’re DONE. You’re FIRED,” as he disinvited Jelly Roll as a participant for the event planned at Trump’s resort on November 17.

“The event is a fundraiser for the Federal Law Enforcement Officers Foundation, a 501(c)(3) that takes care of the families of wounded and fallen officers,” Reyes wrote. “Our organization, which owns the largest police news outlet in the world, is running the event. We’ll be joined by the heads of all of the federal law enforcement agencies, sheriffs, police chiefs and supporters.”

He then added, “We’re formally withdrawing the invitation for Jelly Roll.”

“As the owner of the company, I’m a proud Christian who actually studies the Bible. I’m a husband and a father of four little girls,” Reyes continued.

“And what I saw last week with this self-absorbed ‘artist’ bashing President Trump and Conservatives was not a man who walks in the footsteps of Jesus Christ – it was a man desperately seeking attention and relevancy from the very Godless crowd that has categorically rejected his preaching.”

“The man has lost his way. I don’t hate him. I actually genuinely pity him,” he added.

“Jelly Roll believes in second chances. As a felon, he’s been given one by the judicial system. He may not get one from his former audience. But what he really needs to seek now isn’t forgiveness from President Trump or those who he attacked… but rather from the very God whom he snubbed his nose at while trying to boost his ratings,” the message reads.

“What you did wasn’t strong or in love,” Reyes railed. “It wasn’t the actions of a man. It was the actions of a little boy seeking the approval of man. I’d encourage you to check your heart, brother. Don’t let the ways of this world lead you astray.”

“This isn’t about politics. This is about knowing who you are as a man. And you have much to learn,” he wrote, concluding with, “I very much look forward to honoring God at this gala. I wish you could be a part of it… but I believe that time would be much better spent with you diving into the Bible and finding out who you REALLY are.”

Unfortunately, Jelly Roll continued digging his hole with his own fans as each night of Jimmy Kimmel Live! continued during his week of guest hosting.

After the inevitable backlash came from his mostly Christian and conservative fans, the “Son of a Sinner” singer later doubled down on his intentions to attack the right, and even told offended fans they could feel free to stop listening to his music.

“For those who threatened to stop listening to my music based on my comments last night, I just want to say with conviction: go right ahead,” he said grinning like a jackal.

Still, it is clear Jelly Roll was stung by the backlash because by the end of his week in the Kimmel host chair, he was crying on stage and attempting to claim that he is a “centrist” who sees things wrong with both parties, despite that he never once criticized liberals during his stint as guest host.

The backlash was neither small, nor isolated. In the immediate aftermath of his disastrous stint on Kimmel’s show, Jelly Roll reportedly lost hundreds of thousands of fans who unfollowed him on social media.

Reyes later announced that his group replaced Jelly Roll with country singer Coffey Anderson.

“Coffey won’t just be performing ‘Mr. Red White And Blue’ and ‘America is My Hometown.’ He’ll close out the annual gala with WORSHIP MUSIC honoring God,” Reyes wrote.

National police organization Blue Lives Matter has disinvited Jelly Roll from its fundraising event at Mar-a-Lago after the country singer told supporters of President Donald Trump during a "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" monologue that he did not want them as fans and that they should stop listening to his music.

news.title: Brendan Carr Is ‘Looking at a Lot of Actions’ to Answer Trump’s Call for FCC ‘Punishment’ of Kristen Welker
news.text:
Federal Communications Commission chairman Brendan Carr shared that the regulatory agency is responding to President Trump’s call for NBC journalist Kristen Welker to be met with “rebuke or punishment. The president has alleged that Welker’s reporting that he had a “mixed record” for endorsements this election cycle was done with “purposeful inaccuracy.”

In an appearance on “The Sunday Briefing” on Fox News, the Trump-appointed Carr was asked about the president’s threat against Welker. Carr responded by suggesting that broadcast news channels could face consequences if the agency interprets their reporting to not serve the public, citing “fake polls” designed to “suppress” voters as a potential risk.

“President Trump is over the target. We’re looking at a lot of actions,” Carr said, responding to host Peter Doocy. “There’s a lot of interest right now in fake polls that are out there. The FCC may put guidance out soon to remind broadcasters about their obligations with effect to not airing fake polls, particularly if they’re done to suppress people heading into the fall.”

Carr said: “One thing that President Trump gets, fundamentally, is that broadcast TV is completely different than other forms of distribution, including cable. So many broadcasters right now, they want to break the deal that they cut with the American people. They get billions of dollars in taxpayer (money) — effectively subsidize distribution. What they’re supposed to do in exchange is operate in the public interest, not some sort of narrow partisan interest.”

Last week, Welker reported on the “mixed record” of Trump-endorsed candidates in the year’s primary elections, saying on a local affiliate that, “He, of course, has endorsed a slate of candidates in the primaries. He’s had some mixed results, but most recently, his pick of Senator Darline Graham, of course, the sister of the late Senator Lindsey Graham, was successful in her primary battle, so now she takes on Dr. Annie Andrews in South Carolina.”

Trump lashed out at Welker through a post on his social media platform Truth Social shortly after, writing: “Kristen Welker, the Unpopular ‘Hostess’ of the once great Meet the Press, now considered Meet the Fake Press, just stated that Donald Trump has ‘mixed results’ on his Endorsements of Candidates … How can anyone be allowed to say this, working for freely given Public Airwaves? Results are attached. Because of this purposeful inaccuracy, she will be reported to the FCC for rebuke or punishment.”

While the Trump-endorsed Graham and Mazzei each won GOP nominations for their respective Senate races, other candidates with the president’s backing have suffered losses this primary season, including Rep. Cory Mills (R-Fla.), Rep. Andy Ogles (R-Tenn.), former My Pillow CEO Mike Lindell in Minnesota and Amir Hassan in Michigan.

Trump’s push to turn the FCC towards NBC comes as the federal agency fields the ABC lawsuit, which claims the president’s administration has “waged a retaliatory campaign” against the network over its broadcasts. The suit, filed Aug. 18, further seeks to block the FCC “from taking or threatening to take any action” against Disney, ABC and its eight owned-and-operated television stations in connection with early license renewal applications.

A representative for NBC News declined to comment. When asked to comment on Trump’s initial threat last week, a company spokesperson wrote that “Kristen is one of the best in the business and we stand by her.
news.summary:
FCC chairman Brendan Carr says the president's concerns are "over the target"

news.title: Judge sides with Soros-funded NGO over Trump’s anti-lawfare fund
news.text:
A federal magistrate judge has ordered the administration of US President Donald Trump to disclose the names of those who devised a now-defunct fund for victims of politically-motivated prosecution. The lawsuit was filed by multiple plaintiffs, backed by a Soros-funded NGO.

Critics have argued that the $1.8 billion Anti-Weaponization Fund was designed to funnel taxpayer money to Trump’s supporters who claim they were unfairly investigated by the Justice Department, including those prosecuted over the Capitol Hill riots on January 6, 2021.

On Friday, Judge Ivan D. Davis granted a request that the identities of the masterminds behind the fund be revealed to the plaintiffs and their attorneys, noting that this information must not be made public at this stage.

The DOJ has insisted that the names of those people are “irrelevant” to the case and, moreover, constitute confidential attorney-client discussions or government officials’ deliberations. The Department has also filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit altogether.

Among the plaintiffs who challenged the creation of the initiative are a former federal prosecutor who was fired by the Trump administration after working on cases related to the Capitol Hill riots.

Providing legal support for the lawsuit is the Democracy Forward Foundation – a nonprofit organization that professes to advance “democracy and social progress through litigation, policy and public education, and regulatory engagement.” In May, it was named among the recipients of a five-year $300 million grant from billionaire George Soros’s Open Society Foundations (OSF), according to Inside Philanthropy.

The DOJ announced the creation of the fund in May as a part of a settlement agreement between Trump and the Internal Revenue Service (IRS). Under it, Trump and several members of his family, along with the Trump Organization, agreed to drop their lawsuit over a leak of their tax returns. In exchange, the Anti-Weaponization Fund was to be established to provide redress to “victims of lawfare and weaponization.”

“The machinery of government should never be weaponized against any American, and it is this Department’s intention to make right the wrongs that were previously done,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said at the time.

The Trump administration argued that there was a legal precedent for such an initiative, citing a $760 million fund created under former President Barack Obama to redress racism-related claims against the federal government.

However, faced with criticisms from both Democratic and Republican members of Congress, Blanche declared the fund “dead” in August.
news.summary:
A federal judge has ordered the Trump administration to identify people behind the now-defunct fund for victims of political prosecution

news.title: Trump pushes US Supreme Court to revive blocked mail ballot rule as voting begins
news.text:
US President Donald Trump’s administration has again asked the US Supreme Court to allow new Postal Service rules for mail ballots to take effect ahead of November’s midterm elections.

According to CNN, the emergency appeal filed Sunday follows a federal judge’s decision to indefinitely block the USPS plan. 

The administration withdrew an earlier appeal after filing the new request “to simplify proceedings,” the Justice Department said.

The dispute comes as North Carolina has already begun sending mail ballots, with Alabama and several other states expected to follow this month.

“Once those ballot envelopes enter the mailstream, there is no retrieving them,” the Justice Department told the Supreme Court.

The proposed rules would require state and local election officials to upload lists of mail voters to a portal and place special tracking barcodes on ballot envelopes.

The administration says the measures are needed to improve ballot security. However, 23 Democratic-led states and voting rights groups have challenged the plan, arguing it could disenfranchise voters.

“With fewer than 60 days to go before the November election, there is not a shred of evidence that states could comply with it without disenfranchising voters who rely on mail ballots,” ACLU Voting Rights Project director Sophia Lin Lakin said to CNN.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson has ordered challengers to respond by Wednesday.

news.title: REVEALED: Donald Trump's FULL itinerary in Ireland - all his stops, exactly who he's meeting... and the colossal security operation that will see him skip the Phoenix Park to sleep in a bed that he owns in Co Clare
news.text:
The US Secret Service will oversee a massive security operation to ensure Donald Trump can sleep at his Doonbeg Hotel following a packed day of official meetings when he arrives in the country next weekend, the Mail can reveal.

Trump will be flown to Co. Clare, accompanied by two helicopter gunships, after meeting with most Cabinet members and hosting the first press conference by a US president here since George Bush visited in 2004.

The US president will touch down in Dublin Airport in his new Air Force One Boeing 747-8 – provided by the Qatari government – on Saturday morning, the day after the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks.

Once he lands, the biggest security operation in the history of the State will swing into action.

Trump will be greeted at Dublin Airport – the runaway at Baldonnel is not big enough to accommodate his €400million plane – by the Tánaiste, Simon Harris, before being flown to the Phoenix Park in the Marine One Sikorsky helicopter. 

Two Blackhawk gunships will escort Marine One from Dublin Airport to Arás an Uachtaráin, where – as first revealed in the Mail – Trump will have a short courtesy meeting with President Catherine Connolly.

He will then travel in the bullet and bomb-proof US armoured Cadillac limousine – known as ‘The Beast’ – the short distance to the State Residence at Farmleigh, where he will hold a bilateral meeting with Taoiseach Micheál Martin.

However, the US president will not stay at Farmleigh overnight.

Instead, sources familiar with the security operation said Trump is determined to spend the night at the presidential suite in his family-owned hotel in Doonbeg, which hosts the Irish Open golf tournament next weekend.

US Security Service sources said Trump will again board Marine One for the short trip back to Dublin Airport, again accompanied by the two gunships.

He will then be flown by Air Force One to Shannon Airport, where he will be met by a second group of armoured helicopters, which were transported to the west of Ireland in an enormous Boeing C-17 Globemaster military cargo aeroplane on Thursday.

On the final leg of his cross-country journey, Trump will fly to Doonbeg, where he will make a dramatic entrance as the curtain falls on the third and penultimate day’s play of the Irish Open.

On Thursday, the Mail met with the members of the large US Secret Service detail who have been on the ground in Co. Clare for more than two weeks.

One experienced security official – who was in Ireland for Trump’s previous visit in 2019 – said virtually all the US president’s travel will be done by air.

They told the MoS: ‘We are conscious of Ireland’s lack of adequate air power, which actually makes ground travel more security deficient. It is far better for our purposes that the president travels everywhere by air.’

The Government views Trump’s decision to hold meetings with President Connolly and the Taoiseach – as well as most Cabinet ministers at the Ambassador’s residence – as a ‘diplomatic triumph’.

One minister told the MoS: ‘The President of the United States doesn’t fly to small countries like Ireland and hold meetings with their Government very often.

‘Indeed, I can’t think of any other similar instance, for a country lacking significant strategic importance, so this is something that many other countries would be envious of.

‘We, the Government, do not view it as an opportunity to be making the kind of points the hard-left would like to be.

‘This is high-level diplomacy and will be conducted to serve the interests of Ireland.’

Other senior Government sources welcomed the unexpected news that the US president will host a press conference after his meeting with the Taoiseach at Farmleigh.

His predecessor Joe Biden – who has close Irish family links – did not host a press event during his visit to the country in 2023.

As Ireland currently holds the EU Presidency, Mr Martin will be representing the union’s foreign affairs interests, and tariffs are certain to be a subject of discussion, as well as security.

One Government official told the MoS: ‘We expect the press event to be something similar to what the public are used to seeing, which is a “spray” in the Oval Office.

‘There will be a number of questions from the US and Irish press corps to the Taoiseach and president Trump.’

After a packed day of official meetings in Dublin, Trump’s huge security detail will escort the US president to Doonbeg, where the he and First Lady Melania dined in the golf clubhouse during their 2019 visit.

On that occasion, the Mail attended dinner with the couple, when Trump enjoyed fish and chips, which is still on the menu at €29, although Melania will not be joining her husband on this visit.

US administration sources said Trump was determined to stay at his hotel to maximise publicity for his Irish business.

This week, the MoS witnessed US Secret Service personnel reconnoitring locations Trump may choose to visit next Sunday, including, Bunratty Castle, one of the country’s most famous historic buildings.

However, it is expected Trump will remain at Doonbeg to watch the conclusion of the Irish Open, in which his friend and Irish six-time major champion Rory McIlroy will be competing.

The tournament is expected to conclude at around 6pm, but if a playoff is required, it could extend to 7pm.

President Trump will then return by helicopter to Shannon Airport before boarding Air Force One for his return flight to the US.

A massive US security presence was visible throughout the Mid-West this week. A contingent of US Marines is staying at a city centre hotel in Limerick and armed personnel carriers and other vehicles continued to arrive at Shannon this weekend on C-17 aircraft.

A US administration source said: ‘This is a good news trip for President Trump, he does not see the Irish as opponents in any fashion, and he really is keen to see his golf course, Doonbeg. He hasn’t been there in a good few years.

‘The official aspects of the visit have been negotiated by [US Ambassador to Ireland] Ed [Walsh] and far surpass the interaction President Trump had when he visited Ireland in 2019. 

The fact that Ireland holds the EU Presidency does heighten the seriousness of the talks with the Taoiseach, however.’ This week it was widely reported Trump will meet with President Connolly during his visit, a fact highlighted by the Mail two weeks ago.

Despite her past criticisms of the US President, the Government has no concerns about the meeting at Áras an Uachtaráin.

A senior Coalition source said: ‘To be honest, President Connolly is a far less tricky customer for the Government than her predecessor Michael D Higgins.

He was liable to say and do anything and we certainly couldn’t have permitted a meeting between he and President Trump. Michael D could not have resisted a publicity grabbing clash.’

They added: ‘President Connolly is only at the beginning of her term, and she seems to be enjoying it, so she will be all sweetness and light. She has not put a foot wrong in her Presidency and we don’t expect any hassle there.’
news.summary: With his Men in Black already working overtime, once the US president lands, the biggest security operation in the history of the State will swing into action.
news.author: Editor,John Lee

news.title: The Falklands claim, one of the few issues that cuts across Argentina's political divide
news.text:
The Falklands claim, one of the few issues that cuts across Argentina's political divide

The sovereignty claim over the Falklands is one of the few points of consensus that cuts across Argentina's political fracture, known locally as “la grieta”, a polarisation that splits the country into two opposing camps on almost every public question. That cross-cutting quality explains both its constant presence in popular culture and its recurrence in political discourse.

Political scientist Mariana Altieri, author of a comparative study of the archipelago and Gibraltar, links that centrality to Argentina's founding narrative. “When Argentina became independent from Spain, the islands were part of it and then they were taken from us, and that is associated with Argentina's trauma, with what could have been and is not,” she says. Anthropologist Rosana Guber, a researcher at Conicet and a specialist on the 1982 conflict, suggests understanding it as a symbol comparable to the flag or the anthem: “They speak to people who may hold different positions on everything else.”

The attachment is strongest in the far south. In Río Grande, less than 600 kilometres from the islands and almost 12,800 from British shores, the outline of the archipelago appears on school uniforms, sports kit and numerous murals. The anthem of Tierra del Fuego province is the March of the Malvinas, and the vigil held every April 1 draws up to 20,000 people, according to historian Esteban Rodríguez.

Concrete knowledge of the territory, by contrast, is limited. Journalist Nicolás Cassese, who has travelled to the archipelago three times, estimates that fewer than 1% of Argentines have visited it. “Of Messi and Maradona we have an enormous amount of information, and of the islands we know almost nothing,” he says. He recounts that when he published a novel set in Stanley some readers did not recognise the place name, and notes the settlement was founded in 1845, when the British already administered the islands, and that Argentines themselves used that name for decades.

That consensus has made political use easier. President Javier Milei addressed the nation on Thursday following Donald Trump's remarks about a possible review of US neutrality, announcing sanctions on companies operating in the area without Argentine authorisation and the construction of a military base in the south. The opposition noted that a 2011 law already provides for such sanctions and that construction of the base had begun before his own government halted it. The La Plata veterans' centre criticised his use of the claim as a “lifebelt”. In 2025 Milei had argued that islanders should decide: “We hope the islanders choose to vote for us with their feet.” Altieri describes Thursday's speech as “a 180-degree turn”.

The United Kingdom has administered the archipelago since 1833 and maintains that its status depends on the wishes of its inhabitants. In the 2013 referendum, 99.8% of voters chose to remain a British overseas territory, with three votes against.
news.summary: The sovereignty claim over the Falklands is one of the few points of consensus that cuts across Argentina's political fracture, known locally as "la grieta", a polarisation that splits the country into two opposing camps on almost every public question. That cross-cutting quality explains both its constant presence in popular culture and its recurrence in political discourse.

news.title: Donald Trump brutally mocked after unveiling bizarre dark new haircut
news.text: Donald Trump has sent the internet into meltdown after stepping off Air Force One sporting a bizarre dark new trim. The 80-year-old President, notoriously sensitive about his iconic golden mane , was snapped touching down in Morristown, New Jersey, before heading off for a weekend at his Bedminster golf club. Dressed in his standard navy suit and bright yellow tie, it wasn't his outfit that had onlookers doing a double-take, but his shockingly darker locks . Social media users and commentators immediately jumped on the opportunity to roast the politician's fresh look. Journalist Aaron Rupar took to X (formerly Twitter) to express sheer disbelief, writing: "What is [sic] the world is going on with Trump's hair ?" Meanwhile, high-profile lawyer and fierce Trump critic George Conway took things a step further, joking: "Something needs to be done about his hair under the Twenty-Fifth Amendment." Media commentator Yashar Ali admitted he had to check the pictures twice before posting: "The hair???? If I hadn't pulled the photos from Getty Images myself, I wouldn't have believed it." Former Republican congressman Adam Kinzinger couldn't contain his reaction either, simply posting: "You have got to be kidding me." The ruthless online teasing kept piling up as users weighed in on the sudden dye job. Molly Jong-Fast said: "Trump is now a brunette!" Anne Lamott sarcastically wrote: "I love it. So youthful. Very Pierce Brosnan." Paul Rudnick took a darker jab, saying: "Trump told his stylist, 'I want to look like serial killer Rex Heuermann.'" Trump's hair has been a source of wild online theories and late-night TV talk show debates for decades, with critics long alleging he wears a wig. Last month, eyebrows were raised when his locks appeared brighter and thicker than usual during a public appearance. Addressing the relentless rumours directly during a speech in the White House Rose Garden, Trump previously said: "For years, I had to suffer with people saying, 'He wears a wig.' I don't wear a wig." Whether it's a dye job gone horribly wrong or just a dramatic new style choice, Trump's latest look has ensured all eyes remain firmly on his head.
news.summary: Donald Trump has been ruthlessly mocked online after stepping off Air Force One with a shocking, dark new haircut replacing his signature golden mane
news.author: Liam Randall

news.title: Flight price rises due to ‘foolish leaders’ starting wars, Virgin’s Branson says
news.text:
Virgin Group founder Sir Richard Branson has blamed flight price rises on "foolish leaders" starting wars, in a thinly veiled reference to the US-Israel conflict with Iran.

Middle East tensions have choked the production and transportation of millions of barrels of oil, causing a surge in the price of car and jet fuels, which are made from oil.

In May, Virgin Atlantic added a fuel surcharge to ticket prices in response.

US President Donald Trump has repeatedly defended the conflict as necessary for long-term peace and security.

However, Sir Richard said there was "no need" for the war.

"The Iran conflict was completely unnecessary. There was a nuclear agreement between Iran and the rest of the world, negotiated by President Obama and many Europeans.

"It was working, so there was no need to rip it up... And this war has just led to much higher oil prices worldwide. And inflation has been one of the consequences."

The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.

The European benchmark jet fuel price had been hovering around $800 (£590) a tonne, but spiked following the outbreak of the war in Iran, reaching a peak of over $1,800 in April. It has since dropped to around $1,450.

Virgin Atlantic's chief executive, Corneel Koster, told the BBC that for "this level of fuel price" fuel surcharges were "absolutely required", adding that it's "hard to be optimistic at this moment about the situation in the Middle East".

The surcharge Virgin introduced added £50 to an economy-class fare, £180 to a premium-class fare, and £360 to a business-class fare.

Several of Virgin's rivals cut flights in addition to raising fares following the start of the conflict.

In April, analysis from consultancy firm Teneo found the Iran war had led to a 25% increase in air fares.

And this week Ryanair said it would reduce its winter schedule because of higher fuel prices and warned European short-haul fares would "increase materially" if jet fuel prices continue to rise until next summer.

Yet, despite the higher costs, Koster said Virgin did not plan to make any big changes to its winter schedule.

He said winter capacity had already been slightly reduced a few months ago and added that if there was low demand on certain routes "in the depths of winter", there would be some trimming or "capacity discipline", but not "big percentages".

The airline expects to fly 95% of its regular schedule.

Sir Richard was speaking to the BBC as Virgin Atlantic announced it had secured a contract to fly Team GB and ParalympicsGB to Los Angeles for the Summer Olympics in 2028.

The airline took the contract from rival British Airways, which had been doing it since the 2008 games in Beijing.
news.summary: Virgin Group founder Sir Richard Branson has blamed flight price rises on "foolish leaders" starting wars, in a thinly veiled reference to the US-Israel conflict with Iran.
news.author: Abubakar Ibrahim

news.title: Heading to America to bridge the gap in US-China relations
news.text:
Before boarding my flight to Boston late last month, I spent the better part of three days doing something I never imagined I would do in more than 30 years of covering China: scrubbing my phone. Old emails, screenshots, WeChat threads that might be read the wrong way, anything that could be misconstrued in an airport interview room – all deleted, just in case.
I was not being paranoid. I was following advice now routinely passed among Chinese travellers to the United States: carry a clean phone, or better yet, a burner. American officials, academics and business travellers headed into China have long been told the same thing. Two sets of citizens, one shared instinct – that what is on your phone could get you into trouble on the other side.
As it turned out, my entry into the US was swift and unremarkable. No locked room, no confiscated devices, none of the horror stories that have circulated among Chinese academics in recent years. The gap between what I feared and what happened was, in miniature, what I have spent 35 years writing about: the gap between perception and reality in US-China relations. It is also the reason I am here.
Beginning this month, I take up a one-year appointment as a senior visiting scholar at the Rajawali Foundation Institute for Asia at the Harvard Kennedy School. My purpose is straightforward to state and harder to fulfil: to sit down with American thought leaders across the political spectrum and ask them where they think this relationship is headed, and whether conflict is as inevitable as it now appears.
To understand why this question matters so much, a brief look back is useful. The relationship began its current downward spiral in 2018, when the first Trump administration launched its opening salvo in the trade war. At the time, the confrontation felt sudden and jarring. It was not, in fact, sudden at all. Grievances had been quietly accumulating for decades across government, industry, trade, academia, science and technology. What changed in 2018 was that those grievances finally found their outlet.
Layered on top were structural anxieties. In Washington, there is the perceived erosion of American primacy in manufacturing and superpower status. In Beijing, there is a mirror-image worry: that a declining but still-dominant America, unwilling to accept the reality of a rising China, is bent on containing its development, through tariffs, technology export controls and alliances built for that purpose.

That mutual anxiety, in turn, fed less rational forces on both sides of the Pacific: incomplete narratives, hostile rhetoric, rumour dressed as fact, all doing damage to how each public sees the other. In Washington, there is a wry observation that American politicians agree on almost nothing except the need to get tough on China. In China, public sentiment towards the US has turned sour.
The goodwill accumulated over decades of engagement has largely evaporated, replaced by mutual suspicion and precaution – of which my scrubbed phone is a small but telling example.
None of this is to dismiss the seriousness of the moment. In the past fortnight alone, US Treasury officials have floated the possibility of sanctioning Chinese banks over their dealings with Iran, a suggestion that drew a sharp pushback from Beijing.
Long Guoqiang, deputy director general of the Development Research Centre of the State Council, a leading government think tank, captured the prevailing mood in Beijing when he warned recently that the US remains “the biggest external source of uncertainty affecting China’s path to modernisation”. He argues that American containment of China will persist and intensify over the long run, notwithstanding the trade war truce.
Long’s warning is not wrong. But a truce, however temporary, is also an opening. After their Beijing summit in May, President Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump are set to meet three more times this year: Xi is expected in Washington later this month, with further encounters likely on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation and G20 leaders’ meetings in November and December.

Much of the coverage of these meetings will, understandably, focus on tangible deliverables – deals on trade, investment, technology. But Beijing and Washington might also use the moment to look at the bigger picture, along three tracks that receive far less airtime than they should.
On global challenges, can both powers still cooperate on climate change and future pandemics, even if the current US administration shows little enthusiasm for the former?
On engagement, law enforcement cooperation – against transnational crime, the booming scam-centre operations along China’s periphery, and the flow of fentanyl precursor chemicals into North America – is a shining example. Quiet cooperation on precursor chemicals continued even through the worst of the trade war, proof that narrow, mutually beneficial arrangements can survive broader hostility when both sides see a direct interest in results.
I am a clear-eyed optimist – clear-eyed about the depth of the pessimism baked into this relationship, but unwilling to accept that Washington and Beijing are destined for conflict

And on global regulation, can the two governments find common ground in governing artificial intelligence, space and other emerging technologies?
Right now, discourse in both capitals dwells overwhelmingly on the negative. Far less is said about where cooperation remains not just possible but necessary.
That is what I intend to spend the next year finding out. I am, by long habit of observation, a clear-eyed optimist – clear-eyed about the depth of the pessimism baked into this relationship, but unwilling to accept that Washington and Beijing are destined for conflict. From Cambridge, I plan to reach beyond the think tanks most familiar to a China watcher, including into quarters not typically friendly to Beijing’s view of the world, setting aside my instincts and assumptions as best I can.
What will I find by the time this fellowship ends? I do not know. But having spent three decades chronicling how perception so often diverges from reality in this relationship, I remain hopeful that reality, properly examined, still leaves room for two great powers to coexist – durably, and peacefully – for everyone’s sake.

news.title: Trump wants New Mexico to be renamed ‘New America’, after ‘Lake America’ fiasco
news.text:
US President Donald Trump has appeared to suggest renaming New Mexico “New America”, days after signing an executive order changing the US federal name for Lake Ontario.

Trump posted a map of New Mexico on Truth Social on Sunday showing the word “Mexico” crossed out in red and replaced with “America”. 

The White House later reposted the image on its verified X account.

Neither Trump nor the White House explained the post or announced a formal proposal to change the state’s name, Fox News Digital reported.

The post follows Trump’s executive order renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America” for US federal use amid heightened trade tensions between the United States and Canada.

Trump also renamed the Gulf of Mexico the “Gulf of America” for federal use early in his second term.

However, a US president cannot unilaterally rename a state through executive action. No formal process to change New Mexico’s name has been announced.

The name New Mexico predates US statehood by centuries. Spanish explorers used “Nuevo México” as early as the late 1500s. 

The territory retained its name after becoming part of the United States in 1848 and officially became a state in 1912.

news.title: Trump suggests renaming the state of New Mexico in Truth Social post
news.text:
President Donald Trump suggested renaming New Mexico to New America in a Truth Social post over the holiday weekend. 

The move follows previous executive orders by Trump that renamed the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America and Lake Ontario to Lake America. 

While Apple and Google updated their mapping apps to reflect Trump's changes for US users, MapQuest refused to comply and experienced a surge in downloads. 

Trump's geographic rebranding efforts have drawn criticism from groups like Republicans Against Trump, even as he posted a separate image claiming US ownership of the moon. 

A recent poll revealed that 73 percent of Americans feel Trump has not paid enough attention to the nation's most critical problems.
news.author: Rachel Dobkin

news.title: Parisi dhe Berlini në përplasje, Kallas nën presion
news.text:
Paris, 6 shtator Zhurnal.mk – Franca dhe Gjermania kërkojnë që Shërbimi Evropian i Veprimit të Jashtëm (EEAS) të integrohet në masë të madhe në strukturat e Komisionit Evropian, ndërsa shefja e diplomacisë evropiane, Kaja Kallas, kundërshton fuqishëm humbjen e autonomisë institucionale dhe paralajmëron se një strukturë e tillë do ta bënte politikën e jashtme të BE-së jofunksionale.

Zyrtarë të lartë të BE-së tashmë kanë nisur të shqyrtojnë se cilat funksione të EEAS mund të merren përsipër nga departamentet ekzistuese të Komisionit Evropian, sipas personave të njohur me procesin. Kjo do të përbënte një kthesë për një nga reformat më të mëdha institucionale të BE-së të ndërmarra gjatë dy dekadave të fundit.

Komisioni Evropian po përgatit plane për shkëputjen e shërbimit diplomatik të Bashkimit Evropian nga pushteti ekzekutiv i bllokut, si përgjigje ndaj kërkesave të Francës dhe Gjermanisë për një reformë të thellë të mekanizmit të politikës së jashtme të Brukselit deri në fund të këtij viti.

Kjo nismë ka hasur në kundërshtimin e përfaqësueses së lartë të BE-së për Punët e Jashtme dhe Politikën e Sigurisë, Kaja Kallas, e cila kundërshton planet për shpërbërjen e shërbimit që ajo drejton.

Zyrtarë të lartë të BE-së tashmë kanë nisur të shqyrtojnë se cilat funksione të Shërbimit Evropian të Veprimit të Jashtëm (EEAS) mund të merren përsipër nga departamentet ekzistuese të Komisionit, sipas personave të njohur me procesin. Kjo do të përbënte një kthesë në një nga reformat më të mëdha institucionale të BE-së të realizuara gjatë dy dekadave të fundit.

EEAS nën lupën e qeverive kombëtare

EEAS, i drejtuar nga shefja e diplomacisë së BE-së, Kallas, është vënë nën lupën e qeverive kombëtare të vendeve anëtare, të cilat konsiderojnë se shërbimi po has vështirësi në koordinimin e përgjigjeve efikase ndaj krizave, përfshirë luftën në Ukrainë dhe Iran, si dhe përballjen me politikën e jashtme të presidentit amerikan Donald Trump.

Planet, në të cilat marrin pjesë zyrtarë nga sekretariati i përgjithshëm i Komisionit, si dhe departamentet e tij ligjore dhe buxhetore, synojnë të reduktojnë mbivendosjen e detyrave dhe të harmonizojnë më mirë punën diplomatike të BE-së me kompetencat e Komisionit në fushën e tregtisë, ndihmës, rregullimit digjital dhe teknologjisë.

Ato janë hartuar gjithashtu me synimin për të gjeneruar kursime, ndërsa kryeqytetet kombëtare po i bëjnë presion Brukselit që të shtrëngojë shpenzimet gjatë negociatave për buxhetin e ardhshëm shumëvjeçar të BE-së.

Sipas burimeve të njohura me procesin, nisma nuk parashikon që EEAS të përfshihet në Komisionin Evropian si një drejtori gjigante për politikën e jashtme. Në vend të kësaj, funksionet e tij ekzistuese do të ndaheshin ndërmjet departamenteve të ndryshme, me qëllim rritjen e efikasitetit.

Diplomatët evropianë thonë se kuadri i gjerë për çdo transferim të kompetencave, në mënyrë ideale, mund të dakordësohet në dhjetor, si pjesë e marrëveshjes për buxhetin e BE-së për periudhën 2028–2034.

Presioni për reforma nga Parisi dhe Berlini po rritet

Planet janë ende në fazën fillestare dhe mund të ndryshojnë. Pritet që ato të zhvillohen më tej përpara samitit të liderëve të BE-së muajin e ardhshëm, të cilin Parisi dhe Berlini – dy ekonomitë më të mëdha të BE-së dhe fuqitë kryesore diplomatike – duan ta shfrytëzojnë për të diskutuar idetë për reforma.

Presioni franko-gjerman u intensifikua gjatë verës. Një gazetë franceze fillimisht publikoi opsionet për riformatimin e politikës së jashtme të BE-së, ndërsa më pas, në korrik, pasoi një deklaratë e përbashkët që bënte thirrje për një debat më të gjerë për të ardhmen e Unionit.

Këtë javë, një dokument franko-gjerman bëri thirrje për „integrimin në masë të madhe të shërbimeve të EEAS në strukturat e Komisionit“.

Franca dhe Gjermania kanë propozuar që Kallas të ketë një rol personal më të fuqishëm në çdo strukturë të reformuar, me mbikëqyrje më të madhe mbi portofolin e zgjeruar të marrëdhënieve të jashtme të Komisionit.

Një version më i vogël i EEAS do të mbetej jashtë Komisionit dhe do të mbikëqyrte fusha si misionet paqeruajtëse të BE-së dhe trajnimi ushtarak.

„Ka diskutime dhe shqyrtime të vazhdueshme se si të reformohet dhe forcohet veprimi i jashtëm i BE-së. Duke pasur parasysh mjedisin gjeopolitik, është e qartë se duhet të modernizohemi dhe përshtatemi vazhdimisht për të siguruar që mjetet, strukturat dhe proceset tona të vendimmarrjes të vazhdojnë të mundësojnë veprime efektive. Komisioni është i gatshëm të kontribuojë në këtë diskutim“, theksoi një zëdhënës i Komisionit Evropian.

Kallas lufton fuqishëm për të ruajtur kompetencat

Kallas po udhëheq një përpjekje të fuqishme prapa skenave kundër planeve franko-gjermane për reformimin e shërbimit të saj diplomatik, duke lobuar te kryeqytetet evropiane, shkruan „Politico“.

Fushata e Kallas përfshin bindjen e qeverive të BE-së se problemet me politikën e jashtme të bllokut burojnë nga rregullat e vendimmarrjes me unanimitet dhe zbatimi i dobët i marrëveshjeve të brendshme, dhe jo nga struktura aktuale institucionale, sipas tre zyrtarëve të BE-së të informuar për planet e saj.

Kundërshtimi po udhëhiqet nga sekretarja e re e përgjithshme e EEAS, Kajsa Ollongren, e cila po zhvillon një turne nëpër kryeqytetet e BE-së për të diskutuar propozimet për reforma me qeveritë kombëtare.

Pritet që Ollongren të propozojë edhe krijimin e një grupi pune për shqyrtimin e reformave të mundshme të brendshme.

Aleatët e Kallas konsiderojnë se reforma, e cila synon ta bëjë politikën e jashtme të BE-së më efikase, në fakt mund t’i japë Komisionit Evropian të udhëhequr nga Ursula von der Leyen kontroll më të madh mbi punën që zhvillohet nën drejtimin e shefes së diplomacisë evropiane.

Plani gjerman për bashkimin e shërbimit diplomatik të BE-së me Komisionin Evropian do të forconte ndikimin e presidentes së Komisionit Evropian, Ursula von der Leyen, mbi politikën e jashtme, ka raportuar „Euractiv“.

„Kallas dëshiron ta shtyjë të gjithë procesin sepse nuk dëshiron të jetë një mjet i von der Leyen“, tha një diplomat evropian.

Edhe vetë Kallas ka kundërshtuar publikisht mundësinë që të jetë nën kontroll më të madh nga von der Leyen, pa e përmendur drejtpërdrejt presidenten e Komisionit Evropian.

„Nëse kam dikë mbi vete që në fakt merr vendimet, atëherë kjo nuk funksionon“, deklaroi Kallas këtë javë, pas debatit me ministrat e Jashtëm të BE-së në Wicklow, Irlandë.

Von der Leyen dhe Kallas kanë pasur mosmarrëveshje për disa çështje që lidhen me politikën e jashtme evropiane – nga konflikti ushtarak në Palestinë, te koordinimi i inteligjencës evropiane dhe emërimet e personelit gjatë dy viteve të fundit.
